label: text
text: FOUNDATION STONE: LAID

label: paragraph_title
text: WOMEN AND THE FUTURE OF CHINA.

label: text
text: The foundation stone of the new and larger building which the increasing number of students has necessitated being built in connection with St. Paul's (Girls) College was laid on Saturday afternoon by H.E. the Governor, Sir R. E. Stubbs, K.C.M.G. The site is between Kennedy Roads and Macdonnell Road.

label: text
text: His Excellency, who was accompanied by Mr. T. J. Gaisford-St. Lawrence (Private Secretary), was well on arrival by the Right Rev. C. R. Duppy (Bishop of Victoria), the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall (Chairman of Building Committee), and Miss Woo (headmistress). Amongst others present were Mrs. Duppy, the Rev. W. H. Hewitt and Mrs. Hewitt, the Rev. A. D. Stewart, the Rev. Dr. T. W. Peurce, O.B.E., Mr. E. Ralphs (Inspector of Schools), the Rev. T. B. Powell, Mr. E. Forster, Mr. S. W. Tso, Miss Nell E. Elliott, Mr. Colbonne Little, Mr. and Mrs. C. F. Savage, and Mr. Lam Woo. All the available space on the site was occupied by a large number of others who are interested in education in the Colong, besides subscribers to the building fund, and a full muster of the girls of the College.

label: text
text: The site and the approach to it had been guilty decorated with flags, streamers and greenery, and the solemn proceedings commenced with the signing of the hymn "All hail the power of Jesus' name!" An interesting report was presented by the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall, which was followed by the ceremony of laying the foundation stone by His Excellency the Governor. The Right Rev. C. R. Duppuy offered the dedictory prayer and pronounced the blessing.

label: text
text: The inscription on the foundation stones, one bearing a translation in Chinese characters, was as follows:—

label: text
text: Prior to the stone being lowered, His Excellency placed in the niche below a small brass box containing a document giving the history of the College, also a Hongkong bank note, and silver and copper coins. The silver trowel with which the ceremony was performed was presented to His Excellency as a memento and was inscribed as follows:—

label: text
text: "Presented to His Excellency Sir Reginald Edward Stubbs, K.C.M.G., Governor of Hongkong, on the occasion of laying the foundation stone of the new building for Paul's Girls' School, Honath, June, 1925."

Hon. Mr. Kotewart. /.port.
The Hon. Mr. Kotewart said:—
Your Excellency, my Lord
Bishop, ladies and gentlemen,—
As Chairman of the Building
Committee I have been asked by
the Committee of Management of
St. Paul's Girls' School to give a
short history of the project for
erecting the permanent building
whose foundation stone will pres
sently be laid by His Excellency
the Governor.

label: text
text: From the time of its establishment in 1915, to the present day, St. Paul's Girls' School has always been housed in rented quarters which have never been quite suitable or adequate to its needs. It is at present occupying a house on Cainé Road, which is not only too small for its requirements but has no playground worthy of its name, and is becoming more and more unsuitable as the vehicular traffic on the narrow Caine Road increases. At the beginning of 1923 the Committee came to the keenest realisation of the need for a permanent building when they received from the landlord notice to quit. For a time it looked as if the School had to be closed, no other suitable premises being then obtainable; but fortunately, thanks to the kindness of the landlord, it was permitted to remain on for another twelve months. In June of the same year Miss Woo, the Headmistress, after having secured the promised support of some of the leading Chinese, applied to the Government for a site for a permanent school-building. A Building Committee was subsequently formed, and I was elected to be its Chairman. Within the short space of two months from the date of our application a reply was received from the Government stating that it was prepared to grant to the School the fine and valuable site, on which

label: text
text: we are now standing together with a sum of $50,000 towards the cost of the building, provided that $200,000 was raised for the purpose by private subscription. (Applause). We found no difficulty in raising in four months $100,000 thanks to the unstirring energy and persuasive power of Miss Woo, and to the generosity and assistance of certain public spirited men, particularly Mr. Kan Tongpo and Mr. Lam Woo. (Applause). Though we had found, only half of the requisite sum, the two Committees felt that, judging from the enthusiasm shown by the community, it would be quite safe to have plans of the new building prepared at once. We were fortunate in our selection of the architects, Messrs. Little, Adams and Wood, who threw themselves into their part of the good work with the same zeal and zest as have animated the other workers. (Applause).

label: paragraph_title
text: Worthy of the Colony:

label: text
text: The original estimate of the cost of the building, excluding the formation of the site, was $225,000, but the contract was actually let for $265,000 to Messrs. Hop. Hing Cheong in March, 1921. On the front page of the programme in your hands, is a perspective drawing of the fine building which, when completed, should be worthy of the Colony in every way. Less than four months after the land was handed over by the Government's work on site-formation was begun. This degree of accomplishment could not have been possible but for the hearty co-operation of all concerned. First and foremost in practical help is, of course, His Excellency the Governor to whom we are deeply grateful for the grant of the site and money. (Appause). But for his sympathy, and for his great interest in the education of Chinese girls generally, it is unlikely that we would have been given such a valuable site as this, which is, I believe, worth about $160,000. We are no less grateful to Mr. E. A. Irving, late Director of Education, and to Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, the then Acting Colonial Secretary, for having readily entered into the spirit of the scheme, thus making it a success from the very beginning. (Appause). The latter gentleman was also instrumental in the selection of the site, and in expediting matters in every way. The school is also under a debt of gratitude to Mr. A. H. Hollingsworth and Mr. A. E. Wright of the Public Works Department for the trouble they have taken in connection with the grant of the site, and for the expeditious passing of the plans; and to Messrs. Little, Adams and Wood for the more than ordinary interest they have shown in the building scheme. I can testify to the great trouble which Mr. Colbourne Little, Mr. C. H. Basto, and Mr. C. F. Savage of the Firm have taken in the planning of the building, and the unusually large measure of personal attention they have given to the constructional work. (Appause). I must not omit to express our grateful thanks to the gentlemen who have contributed so liberally towards the building fund. First among these open-handed helpers is Mr. Lee Hysan who has very generously promised us $50,000. (Appause). The other liberal donors are Mr. Lam Woo who, besides giving much of his time to supervising the constructional work, has donated $10,000; (Appause). Messrs. Kan Hung-chiu, Mok Ching-kong, Mok Konsang, Li Sing-kue, Li Tse-fong, Kan Ying-po and Kan Tung-po, who have promised $10,000 each. (Appause). Mr. Kwok Yau-ting and Messrs. Hop Hing Cheong, $5,000 each; Mr. Yeung Wing-tai, $3,000; Messrs. Wong Kwok-shuen, Li Kocn-chun, Fung Ping-shan, Chan Pik-chuen, Li Yuk-tong, Kwok Chuen, Choy Hing, $2,000 each; Messrs. Kwok Si-lau, Li Yau-tsun, Li Wing-kwong, Chan Tin-son, Li Yik-mui, and Leung Yan-po, $1,000 each. (Appause). I must crave the indulgence of the other generous donors if I do not here give their names and contributions. A complete list of all donations will be published in the

label: paragraph_title
text: Higher Education.

label: text
text: As I have said, ladies and gentlemen, the contract for the building itself has been let for $265,000. To this sum have to be added about $35,000 for formation of site and "extras," and about $20,000 for equipment. These figures bring the total expenditure up to $820,000. We have raised, or have been promised, $200,000 besides the Government grant of $50,000, and we are therefore still short of $70,000. You all know the good work that the School is doing; you all know its noble objects and aims; and you all know the imperative need of the times to give to Chinese

label: text
text: Girls the education which this School can give. I do not apologise for repeating here certain remarks of mine, rinde at the annual prize distribution of the School in January, 1924. I then said: "St. Paul's Girls' School fills a niche of its own in our educational structure. It affords a sound Chinese education to Chinese girls, giving special attention to the Classics, to domestic economy, to thrift, and to physical culture, while strictly preserving that sense of propriety which is an inborn characteristic of the Chinese girl. It is, I believe, one of the only two schools in Hongkong—and the larger one—which give a higher education in Chinese to girls." I said further: "To my mind, there is greater need for our girls than even for our boys to know their language well before trying to acquire a foreign language, for the girls of to-day are the potential mothers of the future. It is the mother who first teaches her babies the language of the heart, and it is the mother who exercises the greatest influence on her children in the home.

label: text
text: The aim of this school is so to train the girls as to fit them for that great task. These girls are taught the same and practical wisdom of Confucius, based on the family, and wisely adapted to our social life which has, in fundamentals, changed so little since the days of that great sage. The girls are also brought in contact with the spiritual beauty and virtues of Christ's teaching—meekness, self-sacrifice, loving forbearance, and true kindness. Ladies and gentlemen; these words I used two years ago when appealing to the public for its support, and I find that I cannot do better than repeat them here as my reasons for appealing to it for its further support. Judging from the readiness with which the public has so far responded to our appeals, it is not too much to hope that we may soon be able to raise this sum. Confident though I am in this respect, I must ask all those who have the interest of the School at heart, not to slacken their efforts in helping us to realise this expectation.

label: text
text: I cannot conclude my remarks without giving expression to our grateful thanks to His Excellency the Governor for the honour he has done us by coming here to lay the foundation stone of our permanent building. This is probably the last public ceremony which His Excellency performs prior to his impending departure from these shores, and it seems to me to be peculiarly fitting that it is connected with the higher education of girls in the Colony, in which His Excellency has always evinced such lively interest. (Applause): This school will ever remember him and Lady Stubbs with gratitude and affection for the practical support they have given to it. We wish them good health and happiness, and hope that His Excellency's future career in the Imperial Service will be crowded with ever increasing success. (Applause).

label: text
text: And now, ladies and gentlemen, with our hearts filled with the best hopes of the future, and with trust in the Divine blessing to realise for us the happy anticipations which make glad this hour, I would respectfully, on behalf of the School, ask His Excellency to lay the foundation stone.

label: paragraph_title
text: His Excellency's Remarks

label: text
text: Before proceeding with the work of laying the foundation stone, His Excellency the Governor said that he would like to congratulate Miss Woo very heartily on the success of her efforts in raising the very considerable sums of money required for the School and her untiring energy, which was one of her marked characteristics.

label: text
text: He thanked Mr. Kotewall for the kind references he had made regarding himself and Lady Stubbs, and he regretted that she was not there to take his place in this and other matters connected with girls' schools, as she had a more intimate knowledge than he did. However, he claimed to have some knowledge of the subject and, as Mr. Kotewall had said, he took a great deal of interest in educational matters in the Colony as he had always regarded the growing educational movement in China as one of the most important features of the country's advancement.

label: text
text: He endorsed what Mr. Kotewall had said as regards the desirability and necessity for concentrating first on the Chinese language and Chinese studies, as he was convinced that much has been lost in the East by devoting more time to acquiring a knowledge of Western languages to the detriment of ancient language and literature. He welcomed the idea of having a high grade school where Chinese literature would form an important part of the work. What he (His Excellency) hoped to see, he said, was a faculty of arts at the University

label: paragraph_title
text: THE PRESIDENT POLK'S PASSENGERS.

label: text
text: The s.s. President Polk on her third globe-circling voyage, having been entirely rebuilt and redecorated since her last appearance in these waters, has the following prominent passengers on board:—

label: text
text: Mr. R. E. Heinseiman, prominent lawyer of Rochester, N.Y., en route to the States after a sojourn in Japan.

label: text
text: Mr. C. N. Conover, Chief Engineer of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Surrey at Washington, D.C., is on route to Manila on official business.

label: text
text: Major Dallas W. Shaffer and wife—en route to Manlla where Major Shaffer will be in charge of the making of serum for the extermination of the rinderpest. Major Shaffer is being sent there by the U.S. Army.

label: text
text: Mr.. L. G. Weigel and sister Eleanor, of Roselle, N.J., are en route to Manila to visit their uncle, Major-General Weigel, U.S. Army.

label: text
text: Mr. E. R. Roberts, representing the John Lucas Company, of New York, is en route to Singapore on a business trip.

label: text
text: Mrs. J. L. Gallagher and Mrs. Anna Hogrefe of San Francisco—en route around the world. Mrs. Gallagher is the sister of Mr. H. M. Lorber, Secretary of the Robert Dollar Company.

label: text
text: Mrs. Charles Spear and Mrs. F. S. Mills, of San Francisco, en route around the world. They are the wife and daughter of Mr. Charles Spear, President of the State Harbour Board at San Francisco.

label: text
text: Mrs. Mary Sagar, prominent society leader of San Francisco and Napa, California, en route around the world.

label: text
text: Mr. J. J. Cutter, Prune King of California, en route around the world.

label: text
text: Sir Henry S. Patten and family of Alhambra, California, en route to Marseilles. Mr. Patten is a prominent lumberman in Southern California.

label: text
text: In addition to those named there are many other tourists taking advantage of the excellent accommodations and service which the President Polz offers, and a goodly number are joining the ship here and at ports farther south.

label: text
text: It was because of Maurice Flynn's splendid work in the making of "The Last Trail" from Zane Grey's fine novel that William Fox at once promoted him to stardom. And by the same token. "The Last Trail" proved to be so fine a photoplay—so powerful a screen drama—that William Fox decided to hold it back a while and include it in the list of super-specials to be issued this year.

label: text
text: This fine film is now showing at the World Theatre.

label: paragraph_title
text: DRIVE IN TRAP.

label: paragraph_title
text: ASYLUM MAN'S DAY OUT.

label: text
text: Early one morning an inmate of Carmarthen Asylum who had escaped was observed walking in Linnelly, nearly 20 miles distant, by Police-Constable Hall.

label: text
text: The mall, who is passionately fond of horses, observing a pony and governess car in the hospital grounds, jumped into the vehicle and drove off with evident pleasure into the country. The county police soon circulated the runaway's description.

label: text
text: He appears to have had a good time during his 24 hours' freedom, for he drove through towns and villages until he reached Llanelly the same night, where he put up in the Stepney Hotel, the leading hostelry in the tin-plate town.

label: text
text: Having, stabled the pony, he suuntered, through the streets and when challenged by the constable he readily admitted his identity and was handed over to a mental hospital attendant none the worse for his little escape.

label: text
text: In conclusion, His Excellency paid a tribute to Miss Woo for the capable manner in which she imparted education, and hoped that under her guidance the pupils would add to the list of educated women of the Colony, on which the future of China mostly depended. (Applause).

label: text
text: The ceremony closed with three cheers for His Excellency.

Moscow, June 6.—The Kieff military tribunal has concluded the trial of the members of the anti-Soviet organization, “Russia for Russians” headed by the ex-Tsarist General Belavin, who is accused of military espionage on behalf of Poland. Belavin Ivanoff who was an official on the staff of the Ukrainian Red Army, and the woman intermediary Nina Krzeczkovska are sentenced to death. Twelve are variously imprisoned and one acquitted. Belavin allegedly described himself as the ideological enemy of the Soviet and admitted the charge.—Reuter.
